sentences.t: Morris Chang wanted to be a novelist.

He was born in Ningbo, near Shanghai, in 1931, and his childhood was an itinerary of retreats: Nanjing for his father's banking work, Canton, Hong Kong until the Japanese bombing began hours after Pearl Harbor, then Chongqing in the southwest - three wars by the time he was seventeen.
In 1949, with an uncle's help in Boston, he arrived at Harvard.
"My reaction entering Harvard was sheer ecstasy, almost disbelief," he recalled decades later.
The writing dream died of arithmetic: "In the early '50s in the United States, there were Chinese laundrymen, Chinese restaurateurs, Chinese engineers, and Chinese professors.

Those were the only respectable professions for Chinese - no lawyers, no accountants, no politicians." He chose engineering, decided Harvard's general education would not land a top job, and transferred to MIT for mechanical engineering - "the most general of the specialties" (the IEEE's 2011 profile; Stanford's account).

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology gave him two degrees and one failure that mattered: he flunked the PhD qualifying exam - "I simply didn't study hard enough," he says - and went looking for work.
Ford offered $479 a month.
Sylvania Electric Products' tiny semiconductor division offered $480.
Chang asked Ford to beat it; Ford refused; the extra dollar put him in transistors.
It was 1955, and the industry he would reshape twice barely existed (the IEEE profile).
Sylvania put him on germanium transistors, and his first fix was mechanical: assembly-line soldering heat was killing the devices, so he devised a way to attach the wires with indirect heat.
He did not yet understand semiconductor theory, so he taught himself from William Shockley's 1950 textbook, Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors - with an unusual tutor.
A senior Sylvania engineer spent his evenings drinking at the bar of the Ipswich hotel where Chang lived; Chang would study upstairs, then carry his questions down.
"He didn't solve all my problems, but he solved enough so I could move ahead.
He was my main teacher" (the IEEE profile).
Texas Instruments hired him in 1958, and handed him the problem that made his name.
TI was manufacturing four transistors for IBM to IBM's design and process - in effect an early foundry deal - and one of them would not yield.
IBM's own pilot line got ten percent at best; Chang's line got zero, occasionally two or three.
He tinkered for four months - furnace temperature, time, alloys, diffusion materials - until the yield jumped past twenty percent.
TI's president learned his name; IBM sent engineers, convinced he had been lucky, and left convinced he had not.
At twenty-eight he had his first department.
At thirty, TI paid his way through a Stanford PhD, tuition and full salary.
By 1964 he was back in Dallas; soon three thousand people reported to him (the IEEE profile; Stanford's account).
Chang's first revolution was commercial, not technical.

At TI he championed pricing ahead of the cost curve: sell chips cheap before the yields justify it, take the losses early, win the volume, and let the manufacturing learning that volume brings deliver the profit later.
The idea was controversial inside TI; it is now how the entire industry prices.
By 1972 he ran all of TI's semiconductor business - the largest in the world - and he expected, not unreasonably, to run the company one day (the IEEE profile; Stanford's account).
Then TI fell for consumer electronics - calculators, watches - and in 1978 it moved its best semiconductor manager to run it.

Chang was proud of Speak & Spell, the talking toy built on the world's first single-chip speech synthesizer, but the posting rested on a theory he came to reject: that a good manager can manage anything.
"I think he was wrong," he says of the chairman who believed it.

"In the semiconductor business, it's just technology and costs; in consumer, technology helps, but it's also the appeal to consumers, which is a nebulous thing." By 1983 he was sidelined in a staff job - "quality and people effectiveness" - and he resigned.
A year as president of General Instrument in New York ended the same way when the company preferred buying businesses to building them.
"After these two setbacks, at TI and at GI, I did not think that my aspiration to be the CEO of a major U.S.
company was in the cards" (the IEEE profile).
The offer that changed the industry came from a government he barely knew.
K.T.

Li, the architect of Taiwan's technology policy, had met Chang years earlier over a TI assembly plant; now he wanted Chang to run the Industrial Technology Research Institute, the island's research lab.
Nearly everyone Chang knew told him not to go; his wife thought he had lost his mind.

He went in 1985, aged fifty-four, and promptly broke the "iron rice bowl" - the assumption that a government job was for life - putting the weakest two percent of performers on probation and pushing the lab toward industrial contracts.
Hate mail poured in to Taiwan's legislators.
"They considered me a foreigner who suddenly became their boss.
They were scared of me" (the IEEE profile).
Then Li returned with the real proposal: the government wanted Taiwan to have a semiconductor company, and it wanted Chang to build it.
The odds were absurd.
ITRI's best process was three micrometres; the industry leaders were at one and a half - two generations ahead.
TI dominated, Intel was rising, and NEC, Fujitsu and AMD were strong.

Chang's summary of why he said yes anyway is a movie line: "It's like in The Godfather - an offer you can't refuse." Refusing, he explains, would have marked him in Taiwan as a man without ambition (the IEEE profile).
The strategy took weeks of thought and inverted the industry's structure.
In the mid-eighties perhaps fifty "fabless" design companies existed, and they bought manufacturing from the giants - Fujitsu, IBM, NEC, TI, Toshiba - as a side business.

The giants drove brutal bargains: they often demanded the design itself as part of the contract, could launch a competing chip if the product succeeded, and ran the small firms' wafers only when they had spare capacity.
Chang's idea: a manufacturer that designed nothing and sold nothing of its own, so it would never compete with its customers and never bump them.
Taiwan's weaknesses - no design culture, no marketing - would stop mattering; its manufacturing discipline would be the edge.
"At the time it was really a solution looking for a problem," he admitted later, "because nobody wanted just the 'maker' function" (the IEEE profile; Stanford's account).
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company opened in February 1987 with $220 million - half from the government, half raised outside, Philips the anchor investor.
Its first customers were the giants themselves, happy to offload trailing-edge chips they no longer wanted to tie up fabs making.
The founders' own economics were as unusual as the model: Chang received no stock for creating the company.
Years later, still absent from Taiwan's rich lists, he shrugged: "I like to measure a person's wealth as a portion of the shareholder wealth he created.
On that basis, I made out really, really poorly" (the IEEE profile; TSMC's own company profile).
What the pure play unleashed was a generation of companies that could not previously have existed.

Broadcom, Marvell, Nvidia and Qualcomm "started with us when they were small," Chang says; a fabless startup now needed a few million dollars, not a few hundred million for a fab, in the words of Stanford's engineering dean.
The fabless industry went from fifty firms to uncountable.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang wrote to Chang - letters, "the only way I had of contacting him" - and the two companies grew up together; TSMC has made essentially all of Nvidia's chips since (the IEEE profile; Stanford's account).

The numbers, four decades on: in 2025 TSMC manufactured 12,682 distinct products on 305 process technologies for 534 customers, running six 12-inch GIGAFABs in Taiwan plus fabs in Nanjing, Arizona, Japan and elsewhere, with Dresden under construction.
In the second quarter of 2026 it held 72.5 percent of the global foundry market - Samsung, second, had 5.9 (the company profile; TrendForce's count via Focus Taiwan).

The quarter reported last month: revenue of $46.72 billion, up 41.2 percent on the year; a gross margin of 66.4 percent; the new two-nanometre process already eight percent of wafer revenue; and a sixth consecutive record profit, with fourth-quarter revenue guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion (the earnings release; the quarter's coverage).

Chang has a theory of why TSMC worked in Taiwan, and it is not a theory about chips: good technicians from trade schools who aspire to the work, low turnover, and the whole industry concentrated in one place so that learning compounds.
"It works, the learning curve, the experience curve, it works only when you have a common location," he told an MIT audience in 2023.
"Learning is local." The advantages Taiwan holds, he notes, America held in the 1950s and 1960s; someday they may belong to India, Vietnam or Indonesia.
On the politics that now surrounds his company he is economical: "Without national security, we will lose everything, everything that we value.
By all means, let's avoid even a Cold War, if we can" (MIT's account of the talk).
This paper ran the experiment of his legacy again on Tuesday night.

Nvidia reported the first record quarter of its post-founder era - $115.8 billion of revenue, well above the $109.1 billion analysts expected (CNBC's tally) - and essentially every chip in that number came out of Morris Chang's factories, as they have for three decades.

The man who made it possible founded it at fifty-five, after two careers had ended under him; everyone he knew told him not to go to Taiwan; he went because, by his own account, he had little left to lose.
The industry calls his invention the pure-play foundry.
The plainer description is the one on the building in Hsinchu: a company that only makes other people's chips, and has never once competed with a customer (the IEEE profile; TSMC's earnings release).
